about: A command-line tool that tells you which AI models will run on your computer's hardware.

prs.title: Updated model lists now spot mixture-of-experts models
prs.broken: Some AI models use only a small part of themselves per word. When refreshing its list, the tool spotted these only by an old naming style, so newer ones counted as full-size and got far too low a speed.
prs.changed: I made the update read the expert counts each model already lists in its own settings file, as the tool's built-in list already did.
prs.matters: On an 8 GB laptop, one such model now shows about 147 tokens a second instead of 25, and bigger ones get the memory-saving option they qualify for.

prs.title: Big models in a fixed format get an honest memory estimate
prs.broken: Some large models only come in one compressed format. The tool sized them as if a smaller format existed, so it called a model a good fit when it needed far more memory than the computer had.
prs.changed: I made the tool size these models in the one format they actually ship in, as it already did elsewhere.
prs.matters: People no longer download a huge model the tool said would run, only to find it doesn't fit.

prs.title: Mac-only models no longer show up on other computers
prs.broken: Some models only run on Apple's Mac chips. The tool spotted them by a word in the name, but one big publisher of them doesn't use that word, so hundreds appeared on Windows and Linux.
prs.changed: I made the tool also treat everything from that publisher as Mac-only, as other parts of it already did.
prs.matters: On Windows and Linux, the list only suggests models that can actually run there.

prs.title: Upgrade advice now matches the tool's own ratings
prs.broken: The planning feature graded models with an older, looser rule. It called a model "Perfect" where the main check said borderline, and its "add this much memory" advice fell short.
prs.changed: I made the planner use the same grading rules as the main check, and sized each upgrade suggestion to reach the rating it promises.
prs.matters: Someone deciding whether to buy a graphics card with more memory gets advice that holds up.

prs.title: The suggested conversation length now fits in memory
prs.broken: The tool reports how much text a model can hold in mind at once. It sized that to fill all of memory, which its own check calls too tight.
prs.changed: I capped that figure at the same 98% limit the rest of the tool uses.
prs.matters: Following the tool's advice no longer pushes a model past the point where it fits.

prs.title: The download tip now names the version that fits
prs.broken: Some huge models keep idle parts in regular memory. For these, the tool picked one compressed version but told you to download a bigger one that didn't fit.
prs.changed: The tool now reports the version it actually picked, and the memory that version really needs.
prs.matters: People download a model their machine can run, not one that is too big for it.

prs.title: It picks a model size that actually fits your card
prs.broken: The tool picked the largest compressed version of a model that filled 98-100% of memory, then rated that same pick "Too Tight", even when a smaller version fit fine.
prs.changed: It now picks only from versions under the 98% limit, so its pick and its rating agree.
prs.matters: On a 24 GB graphics card, 124 models went from "Too Tight" to a version that fits.

prs.title: Search results can now be read by other programs
prs.broken: Asking the search command for machine-readable output was ignored. It printed a table for humans instead, so scripts reading its output broke.
prs.changed: With that option, search now returns a proper list of matching models, or an empty list when nothing matches.
prs.matters: Scripts and AI agents can use search the same way they already use the tool's other commands.

prs.title: Typos in filters are now caught instead of ignored
prs.broken: Mistyping a filter, like "embeddings" instead of "embedding", silently switched the filter off. You got unrelated models back with no warning.
prs.changed: The tool now stops and lists the valid choices when it doesn't recognize a filter value.
prs.matters: A one-letter typo no longer gives you misleading recommendations.

prs.title: Mixture-of-experts models get memory advice for the size it suggests
prs.broken: llmfit tells you which AI models fit your graphics card. For one kind of model, it measured memory at one compression level but recommended another, so a model it called a good fit could be too big.
prs.changed: I made it measure memory at the same compression level it recommends.
prs.matters: The memory number and the verdict now describe the download it tells you to get.

prs.title: Memory needs for DeepSeek-style models are no longer hugely overstated
prs.broken: Some newer models, like DeepSeek-V3 and Kimi-K2, keep their working memory in a compressed form. llmfit sized it as if uncompressed, about 7 to 25 times too big, so it said they would not fit.
prs.changed: I made it size that memory the compressed way these models actually store it.
prs.matters: These models are now rated on what they really need, so people with smaller cards can see they fit.

prs.title: Planning and downloads work when the server runs on a local socket
prs.broken: llmfit can run as a small server that only the same machine can reach. In that mode, its planning and download features, and the dashboard panels that use them, failed with a server error every time.
prs.changed: I made those features accept a local socket connection as coming from the same machine.
prs.matters: The dashboard's planning and download panels now work in that mode too.
